title: What the City settles, by kind of claim
question: What kinds of claims does the City pay to settle, and which kinds are growing?
finding: The Board passed 620 settlements in which the City pays from fiscal 2017 to 2026 (tax refunds left out), naming $325.9 million: $110.3 million in the five years to fiscal 2021 and $215.6 million in the five since. By the titles’ own description the most money went to injury on a street, sidewalk, park or other City property ($64.0 million in 145 files); employment ($52.4 million in 128 files); civil rights violations alleged ($46.2 million in 63 files); damage to a hotel used as a pandemic shelter ($44.5 million in 9 files). Kinds that grew by half or more between the two halves: employment ($12.3 million to $40.1 million); vehicle collision ($10.4 million to $18.6 million); medical or residential care at a City hospital ($2.4 million to $16.1 million). One kind did not exist before: 9 settlements with hotel owners for damage to a hotel used as a pandemic shelter, $44.5 million, all passed in fiscal 2023 (set out under the hotel screens).
how: Board files titled as settlements and passed in fiscal 2017 to 2026 in which the City pays, leaving out tax-refund settlements and standing authorities to settle every claim from one event (both are in the autopilot file). The kind is read from the clause of the title that says what the claim involves, never from a party’s name; 99% of the titles carry such a clause (titles before fiscal 2017 mostly do not, which is why the count starts there). The amount is the figure in the title, counted in the fiscal year passed. No claimant is named or listed.
limits: Each of these was voted on by the Board; a settlement admits nothing. The titles do not name the department, and “injury on City property” covers streets, parks and buildings alike. One large case moves a year’s total, so a kind that doubles may be two cases. Settlements under the City Attorney’s own limit never reach the Board, and judgments after trial are not settlements. That limit was $25,000 until ordinance 205-26, passed on 2 October 2026, raised it to $100,000. Claims by builders appear here among contract disputes; the overruns file reads the same settlements against each contract’s price and is the place to look for them. What would settle the rest: the City Attorney’s yearly claims report by department and cause, which is not among the documents on disk. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
